title: Affirming self-worth reassurance
description: This latent fires on formulaic, second-person affirming statements that reassure the reader of their inherent worth, strength, and right to prioritize their own well-being -- typically opening with 'Remember' or 'You are/deserve' and using stock phrases like 'strong and capable,' 'deserving of love and respect,' or 'prioritize your own needs and well-being.' It activates most strongly on short, template-like affirmations or their sentence fragments (even bare openers like 'Remember' or 'You're') that read like therapeutic pep-talk boilerplate, and less strongly on longer advice sentences that merely touch on self-care or emotional themes without the direct affirming address. It does NOT activate on advice that analyzes a situation, gives concrete action steps, discusses another person's feelings, or makes judgments (e.g. 'NTA', 'you weren't wrong'), even if those sentences occur in the same supportive/therapeutic context -- the key trigger is the direct, formulaic affirmation of the reader's worth/strength/right to self-priority, not general supportive advice.

title: Judgmental verdict on someone's reaction as unacceptable/unreasonable
description: This latent fires on explicit evaluative verdict statements that pass judgment on a person's reaction, behavior, or response as unacceptable, unreasonable, unfair, disproportionate, or unjustified—typically in the pattern '[Person]'s [reaction/behavior/response] was [unacceptable/unreasonable/unfair/disproportionate]', often as a direct, declarative summary sentence (frequently opening with 'However' or 'Your'). It activates most strongly on short, formulaic condemnation sentences that name a specific person or relation (mom, dad, sister, boyfriend, tutor, officer, etc.) and assign a clear negative moral/social judgment to their conduct, and activates more weakly on related hedged or mixed judgments ('understandable but harsh', 'not entirely unjustified'). It does NOT activate strongly on general advice, empathetic reassurance, explanations of underlying psychology, or discussion of the situation's context/consequences that lack this direct 'X's behavior was [negative-judgment-word]' verdict structure, even if they occur in the same advice-column style text.

title: AITA closing verdict prompt
description: This latent fires on the short, formulaic closing question that AITA (Am I The Asshole) post-writers use to hand off judgment to the reader, most commonly the exact phrase 'So, AITA?' but also close variants like 'Now, AITA?', 'So, are you the asshole?', or 'So, what's the verdict?'. It activates specifically on this transitional discourse marker plus verdict-request question, appearing at the end of a narrative right before the audience is asked to render a judgment. It is weaker or absent on the surrounding narrative content, explanations, advice, or even related phrases like 'Am I the asshole?' used mid-text or 'You are not the asshole' as a stated verdict rather than a solicited question -- i.e., it targets the act of soliciting the verdict, not discussing or delivering it.

title: Numbered list item markers
description: This latent fires on the numeral tokens that begin items in an enumerated or ordered list (e.g., '3.', '4.', '9', sometimes followed by '**' from markdown bold formatting). It activates most strongly on bare standalone digits marking list positions, and in the broader activation set also fires on the surrounding list-item text (advice, steps, tips) that follows such numbering. It would not activate on numbers used in other contexts, such as quantities, dates, measurements, or numerals embedded within prose sentences that are not functioning as list enumerators.

title: Short check-in/opinion-eliciting questions
description: This latent fires on brief, formulaic conversational questions that invite the listener to share their feelings or opinion, especially wellbeing check-ins ('Is everything okay?', 'Are you okay?') and generic prompts for input ('What do you think?', 'What's going on?'). It activates most strongly on these short, templated interpersonal questions, often appearing verbatim or as fragments/list markers (e.g., '2.', '3.', 'Can', 'What') that seem to be truncated instances of the same question pattern, likely from advice-giving dialogue suggesting conversation starters. It does not activate on longer explanatory or advisory sentences that discuss feelings, relationships, or strategies in narrative form (e.g., sentences giving advice about how to communicate, describing someone's emotional situation, or listing options), even when semantically related to checking in or asking about feelings—those require substantive content rather than a short, direct question format.

title: Empathetic situation-labeling exclamations
description: This latent fires on short, formulaic sentences that open an empathetic response by labeling the user's situation or feeling with an adjective pair (e.g., 'tough and confusing', 'frustrating and painful', 'wonderful feeling'), typically in the template 'That/This can be a [adj] and [adj] situation/feeling/experience' or 'What a [adj] situation!'. It activates most strongly on these compact validating exclamations that summarize an emotional state before elaborating, including both negative (frustrating, hurtful, isolating) and positive (wonderful, lovely, great) feeling labels. It does not activate on longer explanatory or advice-giving sentences that describe context, give reasons, offer suggestions, or ask follow-up questions, even if they discuss similar emotional topics (e.g., 'It's understandable that you're upset' or detailed reflections on someone's circumstances), since the latent specifically tracks the brief adjective-pair emotional-labeling construction rather than empathy content in general.

title: Advice to communicate openly and calmly
description: This latent fires on advice-giving language that recommends having an open, honest, calm, or empathetic conversation to resolve interpersonal conflict—phrases like 'express your feelings and concerns,' 'approach the conversation calmly,' 'communicate openly,' and 'have an open and honest conversation.' It also activates strongly on the numbered/bulleted list markers (e.g. '2.', '3.', '4. **') that typically introduce such advice items in structured relationship-advice responses, suggesting the latent tracks the templated 'step in a communication-advice list' pattern as much as the semantic content. It does not activate on sentences that merely describe a relationship situation, assign blame, offer non-communication-related advice (e.g. setting boundaries, seeking therapy, reflecting on oneself), or discuss consequences and context without explicitly urging calm, open dialogue.

title: Numbered list item markers
description: This latent fires on the bare numeral (and often trailing period or bold markdown asterisks) that begins an item in an enumerated list, such as '2.', '3.', or '4. **'. It activates most strongly on isolated list-number tokens themselves, regardless of the topic of the list (advice, pros/cons, factors to consider, etc.), and also activates more weakly whenever such numbered markers appear within surrounding text of a list-based response. It does not activate on the textual content of list items, on bullet points using dashes or asterisks alone, on introductory phrases like 'Here are some factors' or 'Let's break it down', or on ordinary sentences that lack an explicit numeric enumeration marker.
